title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
central_claim: Simulated user + agent with domain API tools and policies; success = final database state equals annotated goal state; introduces pass^k reliability metric; gpt-4o pass^8 < 25% in retail.
cite_claim: pass^k is the probability that all k i.i.d. trials of a task succeed, averaged over tasks; tools are deterministic Python functions over JSON databases (retail 115 tasks, airline 50).
location: Abstract; Sec. 3 'Pass^k metric'; Sec. 4 (domain data); Table 1
quote: defined as the chance that all k i.i.d. task trials are successful, averaged across tasks
relevance: Origin of the pass^k metric fiks already reports. Retail domain is where Outcome Monitors [C11] injected faults; replicating that setup gives a directly comparable detection-only baseline. Repo (sierra-research/tau-bench, MIT) is deprecated in favour of tau2/tau3.

title: sierra-research/tau-bench (GitHub repository)
authors: Sierra Research
central_claim: MIT-licensed original τ-bench code; README states the tasks are no longer maintained and points to the τ²/τ³ repo for fixed tasks.
cite_claim: The original τ-bench task set is unmaintained; fixed tasks live in the τ²/τ³ repository, so v1 numbers are not comparable to later versions.
quote: The tasks in this repo are not updated.
relevance: Comparability caveat: if we replicate Outcome Monitors on tau-bench retail we must pin the exact task version they used (seed 20260718, 50 of 115 tasks).

title: τ²-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
authors: Victor Barres, Honghua Dong, Soham Ray, Xujie Si, Karthik Narasimhan
central_claim: Adds a dual-control telecom domain (Dec-POMDP) where user and agent both act on shared state; tasks verified by DB checks and assertion functions; large drops from no-user to dual-control.
cite_claim: Reward is a function of the final global state (DB check, status assertions, NL assertions, communicated info, action matching); retail 115, airline 50, telecom 114 tasks; one trial over all domains with gpt-4.1 as agent and user costs about $40.
location: Sec. 3.1 Dec-POMDP formalism; Sec. 3.3 Task evaluation; Sec. 4.1 Agent settings; Sec. 4.3 Reliability [cost figure: verify exact section]
quote: the fraction of k independent runs that succeed
relevance: Best-fit external benchmark: deterministic state-based grading, native pass^k, cheap, and the substrate of C7 and C8. Not MCP-native: tools are in-process functions, so fiks needs an MCP + HTTP adapter layer to tap upstream calls. Paper does not inject tool faults, so drift must be added by us.

title: sierra-research/tau2-bench (GitHub repository, τ²/τ³-bench)
authors: Sierra Research
central_claim: MIT-licensed harness with mock, airline, retail, telecom, banking_knowledge and intake domains; supports custom agents; frozen task sets with pinned data; τ³ release includes 75+ task fixes.
cite_claim: τ²/τ³-bench is MIT-licensed, supports plugging in custom agents, and ships frozen, pinned task sets; banking grading was fixed in 1.0.1 so earlier banking results are not comparable.
location: README (License; Domains; Agent Developer Guide; release notes)
quote: Judges do not change the task reward.
relevance: License and harness facts for running fiks on τ². MCP is not mentioned in the README, so an MCP wrapper is our cost. [verify exact phrasing of '75+ task fixes' against release notes]

title: τ-bench leaderboard and project site (τ, τ², τ³)
authors: Sierra Research
central_claim: Three generations: τ (2024), τ² (2025, dual control), τ³ (2026: τ-knowledge banking, τ-voice); Feb 2026 audit corrected more than 50 airline/retail tasks; leaderboard reports Pass^1.
cite_claim: In February 2026 the τ-bench team audited airline and retail tasks and corrected more than 50 of them, so pre- and post-audit scores are not directly comparable.
location: Site home page, version history / task-fix note
quote: The original benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction.
relevance: Comparability: our τ² numbers must name the task-set version. Supports a reviewer concern that agent benchmark labels themselves contain bugs.

title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Tengjun Jin, Yada Pruksachatkun, Andy Zhang, Shu Liu, Sasha Cui, Sayash Kapoor, Shayne Longpre, Kevin Meng, Rebecca Weiss, Fazl Barez, Rahul Gupta, Jwala Dhamala, Jacob Merizian, Mario Giulianelli, Harry Coppock, Cozmin Ududec, Jasjeet Sekhon, Jacob Steinhardt, Antony Kellermann, Sarah Schwettmann, Matei Zaharia, Ion Stoica, Percy Liang, Daniel Kang
central_claim: Many agentic benchmarks have task-setup or reward-design flaws that distort performance; the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC) cut overestimation by 33% on CVE-Bench; τ-bench counted empty responses as successes.
cite_claim: Agentic benchmarks can misstate performance through reward-design flaws; τ-bench counted empty responses as successful.
quote: TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful.
relevance: Critique source. Our own bench grader (no-answer = fail, hedged wrong = wrong) should be audited against the ABC checklist; reviewers will ask.

title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
authors: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Peter Kirgis, et al. (31 authors), Arvind Narayanan
central_claim: Standardized parallel harness for agent evals across models, scaffolds and benchmarks, with LLM-aided log inspection that surfaces unreported agent behaviors.
cite_claim: Agent evaluation needs standardized harnesses and log inspection, shifting focus to agents that work reliably in the real world.
quote: shift the focus from agents that ace benchmarks to agents that work reliably in the real world.
relevance: Methodology reference for reporting cost, scaffold and log inspection alongside pass^k; supports reporting per-trial logs and cost.

title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
authors: Zhenting Wang, Qi Chang, Hemani Patel, Shashank Biju, Cheng-En Wu, Quan Liu, Aolin Ding, Alireza Rezazadeh, Ankit Shah, Yujia Bao, Eugene Siow
central_claim: 28 live MCP servers, 250 tools, 104 tasks (56 single-, 30 two-, 18 three-server); rule-based checks plus LLM judge (o4-mini default); gpt-5 best at about 0.75 overall.
cite_claim: MCP-Bench connects agents to 28 live MCP servers with 250 tools and scores task completion with an LLM judge (o4-mini by default); it does not study server instability or tool-output faults.
quote: connects LLMs to 28 representative live MCP servers spanning 250 tools
relevance: Real MCP servers suitable for measuring fiks false-positive rate on clean traffic. Repo is Apache-2.0 (badge) [verify LICENSE file]; judge model hard-coded to o4-mini, which needs an OpenAI/Azure key and limits comparability for an Anthropic-only run. Some servers need free API keys (NASA, NPS, Google Maps).

title: MCP-Universe: Benchmarking Large Language Models with Real-World Model Context Protocol Servers
authors: Ziyang Luo, Zhiqi Shen, Wenzhuo Yang, Zirui Zhao, Prathyusha Jwalapuram, Amrita Saha, Doyen Sahoo, Silvio Savarese, Caiming Xiong, Junnan Li
central_claim: 231 tasks on 11 real MCP servers in 6 domains; format/static/dynamic evaluators, 57.1% dynamic with real-time ground truth; GPT-5 43.72% SR, Claude-4.0-Sonnet 29.44%; Cursor agent no better than ReAct.
cite_claim: MCP-Universe uses dynamic evaluators that fetch real-time ground truth for time-sensitive tasks (57.1% of evaluators), so scores move with the live world.
location: Sec. 1; Sec. 3.3 (domains, Fig. 3); Sec. 3.4 (evaluators, Table 2); Tables 3-5; Sec. 4.3-4.5
quote: dynamic evaluators that automatically obtain real-time ground truth for temporally sensitive tasks.
relevance: Dynamic evaluators are a ready-made independent oracle against live upstreams (GitHub, Yahoo Finance, Google Maps): a natural source of real (not seeded) drift. Costly in keys (SerpAPI, Google Maps, GitHub PAT, Notion) and nondeterministic; GitHub tasks write to real repos (only under vats98754).

title: MCPMark: A Benchmark for Stress-Testing Realistic and Comprehensive MCP Use
authors: Zijian Wu, Xiangyan Liu, Xinyuan Zhang, Lingjun Chen, Fanqing Meng, Lingxiao Du, Yiran Zhao, Fanshi Zhang, Yaoqi Ye, Jiawei Wang, Zirui Wang, Jinjie Ni, Yufan Yang, Arvin Xu, Michael Qizhe Shieh
central_claim: 127 CRUD-heavy tasks over Notion, GitHub, Filesystem, PostgreSQL, Playwright from curated initial states, each checked by a programmatic verify script; gpt-5-medium 52.56% pass@1 and 33.86% pass^4; implicit failures (finished but wrong) are the majority.
cite_claim: In MCPMark, implicit failures (the agent finishes but the final state fails verification) are the majority of errors across models, often above 50%; per-task cost ranges from $0.01 to $9.18 by model.
location: Abstract; Sec. 2.1-2.3; Sec. 3.1 Metrics; Table 2; Sec. 4.2 + Fig. 5 (failure analysis); App. F Table 9 (cost)
quote: implicit failures account for the majority of errors across all models
relevance: Strong fit for read-after-write contracts: state-based verification, write-heavy tasks, pass^4 already reported (comparable to our pass^k). Filesystem/Postgres/Playwright run locally; GitHub/Notion need accounts. Upstreams for Filesystem/Postgres are not HTTP, so fiks's HTTP tap needs a non-HTTP fault-injection path.

title: eval-sys/mcpmark (GitHub repository)
authors: MCPMark team
central_claim: Apache-2.0 harness; each task has a verify.py; isolated environments; Postgres via Docker, Filesystem local, Notion and GitHub require keys/eval org.
cite_claim: MCPMark is Apache-2.0 licensed and scores each task with an automated verification script in an isolated environment.
quote: This project is licensed under the Apache License 2.0
relevance: License and setup cost for running fiks on MCPMark; the local subset (Filesystem 30, Postgres 21, Playwright 25 tasks) needs no third-party account.

title: LiveMCPBench: Can Agents Navigate an Ocean of MCP Tools?
authors: Guozhao Mo, Wenliang Zhong, Jiawei Chen, Qianhao Yuan, Xuanang Chen, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin, Ben He, Xianpei Han, Le Sun
central_claim: 95 daily tasks over a deployable suite of 70 servers / 527 tools; LLM-as-judge; Claude-Sonnet-4 78.95% while most models 30-50%; retrieval errors are nearly half of failures.
cite_claim: LiveMCPBench evaluates 95 real-world tasks over 70 MCP servers and 527 tools with an LLM judge; retrieval errors account for nearly half of failures.
quote: evaluates 95 real-world daily tasks explicitly constructed to stress diverse tools
relevance: Large server pool in a Docker image: useful for a breadth false-positive scan of fiks contracts. LLM-judge outcome makes it weak for measuring correctness of tool data.

title: MCPToolBench++: A Large Scale AI Agent Model Context Protocol MCP Tool Use Benchmark
authors: Shiqing Fan, Xichen Ding, Liang Zhang, Linjian Mo
central_claim: Built from 4k+ MCP servers in 40+ categories; single and multi-step calls; AST and pass@k scoring; real servers whose success rates vary.
cite_claim: The authors observe that real-world MCP tool success is not guaranteed and varies across servers.
quote: the success rate of real-world MCP tool is not guaranteed and varies across different MCP servers
relevance: Supports the premise that real MCP servers fail. Scoring is call-level (AST, parameter match), so it does not observe tool-output correctness; Pay category needs PayPal/Alipay sandbox access.

title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
authors: Chaithanya Bandi, Razvan-Gabriel Dumitru, Ben Hertzberg, et al. (23 authors), Bing Liu
central_claim: 1,000 tasks (500 public), 36 real MCP servers, 220 tools; claim-level rubric with LLM judge, pass at 0.75 coverage; 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-call related.
cite_claim: On MCP-Atlas, 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-call related.
location: Abstract; failure taxonomy section; leaderboard page (April 2026 re-scoring note)
quote: Automated diagnostics show that 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-call related.
relevance: Largest real-server MCP benchmark. Its failure attribution assumes the servers return correct data; fiks targets the residual tool-side faults. Leaderboard was re-scored in April 2026 (new judge, 100-call budget), so older numbers are not comparable.

title: ScaleAI/MCP-Atlas (Hugging Face dataset, public split)
authors: Scale AI
central_claim: 500-task public subset under CC-BY-4.0; harness at github.com/scaleapi/mcp-atlas.
cite_claim: The MCP-Atlas public split (500 tasks) is released under CC-BY-4.0.
quote: This public release is a subset of 500 sample tasks from the MCP Atlas Benchmark dataset.
relevance: License for adapting MCP-Atlas tasks. Harness license not confirmed [verify github.com/scaleapi/mcp-atlas LICENSE].

title: LiveMCP-101: Stress Testing and Diagnosing MCP-enabled Agents on Challenging Queries
authors: Ming Yin, Dinghan Shen, Silei Xu, Sixun Dong, Mian Zhang, Yebowen Hu, Shujian Liu, Jianbing Han, Simin Ma, Song Wang, Sathish Reddy Indurthi, Xun Wang, Yiran Chen, Kaiqiang Song
central_claim: 101 multi-tool queries; a parallel reference agent executes the ground-truth plan to cope with changing tool outputs; frontier models below 60%; seven failure modes.
cite_claim: LiveMCP-101 handles time-varying tool outputs by running a reference execution plan in parallel with the evaluated agent.
quote: Experiments show that even frontier LLMs achieve a success rate below 60%
relevance: Parallel reference execution is a design pattern for an independent oracle on live upstreams; relevant to fiks's 'agreement with upstream' invariant and confirm step.

title: The Tool Decathlon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Diverse, Realistic, and Long-Horizon Task Execution
authors: Junlong Li, Wenshuo Zhao, Jian Zhao, et al. (21 authors), Junxian He
central_claim: 32 applications, 604 tools, realistic initial environments, execution-based evaluation scripts; best model 38.6%.
cite_claim: Toolathlon tasks are strictly verifiable through dedicated evaluation scripts over realistic initial environment states.
quote: Each task is strictly verifiable through dedicated evaluation scripts.
relevance: Alternative state-verified, MCP-based long-horizon benchmark; license and harness not checked [verify].

title: MCP-RADAR: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Evaluating Tool Use Capabilities in Large Language Models
authors: Xuanqi Gao, Siyi Xie, Juan Zhai, Shiqing Ma, Chao Shen
central_claim: 507 tasks across math, web search, email, calendar, file management, terminal; objective metrics incl. operational accuracy and resource efficiency.
cite_claim: MCP-RADAR measures MCP tool use with objective metrics (answer correctness, operational accuracy, efficiency) rather than binary success.
quote: Unlike traditional benchmarks that rely on subjective human evaluation or binary success metrics
relevance: Related work only; assumes correct tools.

title: MCPVerse: An Expansive, Real-World Benchmark for Agentic Tool Use
authors: Fei Lei, Yibo Yang, Wenxiu Sun, Dahua Lin
central_claim: 550+ live, executable tools; most models degrade as the tool set grows, while agentic models gain by exploring.
cite_claim: MCPVerse evaluates agents against more than 550 real, executable tools.
quote: MCPVerse integrates more than 550 real-world, executable tools
relevance: Related work; breadth candidate for false-positive measurement.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
authors: Yangjun Ruan, Honghua Dong, Andrew Wang, Silviu Pitis, Yongchao Zhou, Jimmy Ba, Yann Dubois, Chris J. Maddison, Tatsunori Hashimoto
central_claim: ToolEmu: an LM emulates tool execution so agents can be tested across many tools without real implementations; an LM safety evaluator flags risky failures.
cite_claim: LM-emulated tools enable broad agent testing, but the emulated outputs are not real upstream behavior.
quote: even the safest LM agent exhibits such failures 23.9% of the time
relevance: Contrast: emulated tools cannot produce a real upstream HTTP trace, so they cannot feed fiks's reproduction step.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Jie Zhang, Mislav Balunović, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, Florian Tramèr
central_claim: 97 tasks and 629 security cases where adversarial content in tool-returned data hijacks agents; extensible environment.
cite_claim: AgentDojo is an extensible environment that injects content into tool outputs to evaluate agent robustness; models often fail tasks even without attacks.
quote: AI agents are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks
relevance: Its tool-output injection mechanism could be repurposed to inject silent (non-adversarial) faults; metrics are security-focused, so comparability with fiks is low.

title: ToolBeHonest: A Multi-level Hallucination Diagnostic Benchmark for Tool-Augmented Large Language Models
authors: Yuxiang Zhang, Jing Chen, Junjie Wang, et al., Hayato Yamana
central_claim: Diagnoses tool hallucination via solvability detection, solution planning, missing-tool analysis; Gemini-1.5-Pro 45.3, GPT-4o 37.0 of 100.
cite_claim: Strong models score poorly on recognizing unsolvable tool tasks (Gemini-1.5-Pro 45.3, GPT-4o 37.0 out of 100).
quote: The current advanced models Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o only achieve total scores of 45.3 and 37.0
relevance: Agent-side hallucination; motivates receipts that let the agent say 'could not confirm' (our 'declined' category).

title: RoTBench: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of Large Language Models in Tool Learning
authors: Junjie Ye, Yilong Wu, Songyang Gao, Caishuang Huang, Sixian Li, Guanyu Li, Xiaoran Fan, Qi Zhang, Tao Gui, Xuanjing Huang
central_claim: Five noise levels on tool environments (names, parameters, descriptions) cause large drops in tool selection and parameter filling.
cite_claim: Tool-learning robustness benchmarks perturb tool documentation and inputs, not tool outputs.
quote: Current research predominantly emphasizes LLMs' capacity to utilize tools in well-structured environments
relevance: Shows the 'noisy tools' literature mostly perturbs the call side; fiks targets result-side silent faults.

title: CRITICTOOL: Evaluating Self-Critique Capabilities of Large Language Models in Tool-Calling Error Scenarios
authors: Shiting Huang, Zhen Fang, Zehui Chen, Siyu Yuan, Junjie Ye, Yu Zeng, Lin Chen, Qi Mao, Feng Zhao
central_claim: Benchmark of tool-calling error scenarios (internal model errors and external environment errors) testing whether LLMs identify, diagnose and recover.
cite_claim: CRITICTOOL evaluates whether models identify, diagnose and recover from tool-calling errors.
quote: how to effectively handle such errors, including identifying, diagnosing, and recovering from them
relevance: Agent-side recovery benchmark; explicit errors, not silent wrong data. [verify that external-environment errors include non-throwing faults]

title: Benchmarking Failures in Tool-Augmented Language Models
authors: Eduardo Treviño, Hugo Contant, James Ngai, Graham Neubig, Zora Zhiruo Wang
central_claim: FAIL-TALMS: under-specified queries and unavailable tools; all models except Claude struggle to recognize missing tools/info; human help fixes vague queries but not broken tools.
cite_claim: Human assistance improved results for under-specified queries but not for unavailable (broken) tools.
quote: find all current models except for Claude struggle to recognize missing tools or information
relevance: Supports the claim that broken tools need a tool-side fix, not more agent-side help.

title: Reducing Tool Hallucination via Reliability Alignment
authors: Hongshen Xu, Zichen Zhu, Lei Pan, Zihan Wang, Su Zhu, Da Ma, Ruisheng Cao, Lu Chen, Kai Yu
central_claim: Defines tool-selection and tool-usage hallucination; RelyToolBench; Relign adds indecisive actions (defer, clarify) to cut hallucination.
cite_claim: Allowing indecisive actions such as deferring or asking for clarification reduces tool hallucination.
quote: tool hallucinations, where models either select inappropriate tools or misuse them
relevance: Agent-side; aligns with our grader's 'declined' outcome as a non-hallucinating response.

title: StableToolBench: Towards Stable Large-Scale Benchmarking on Tool Learning of Large Language Models
authors: Zhicheng Guo, Sijie Cheng, Hao Wang, Shihao Liang, Yujia Qin, Peng Li, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun, Yang Liu
central_claim: Virtual API server with caching and LLM API simulators replaces unstable real APIs to make tool benchmarks stable.
cite_claim: Real online APIs make tool benchmarks unstable; StableToolBench caches responses and simulates APIs to restore stability.
quote: Assessing the capability of LLMs to utilise tools necessitates large-scale and stable benchmarks.
relevance: Record/replay precedent for our fixtures; its cache (Apache-2.0 per C11) was used by Outcome Monitors to mine contracts from organic traffic, a candidate corpus for real silent faults.

title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
authors: Harsh Trivedi, Tushar Khot, Mareike Hartmann, Ruskin Manku, Vinty Dong, Edward Li, Shashank Gupta, Ashish Sabharwal, Niranjan Balasubramanian
central_claim: 9 simulated apps, 457 APIs, ~100 fictional users, 750 tasks, state-based unit tests; GPT-4o ~49% normal, ~30% challenge.
cite_claim: AppWorld evaluates agents with state-based unit tests over a controllable simulated app world.
quote: supports robust programmatic evaluation with state-based unit tests
relevance: Second deterministic, state-graded substrate (used by C7 and by Outcome Monitors' held-out study); APIs are REST-like, so an HTTP tap is plausible [verify].

title: ToolSandbox: A Stateful, Conversational, Interactive Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Tool Use Capabilities
authors: Jiarui Lu, Thomas Holleis, Yizhe Zhang, Bernhard Aumayer, Feng Nan, Felix Bai, Shuang Ma, Shen Ma, Mengyu Li, Guoli Yin, Zirui Wang, Ruoming Pang
central_claim: Stateful tool execution with implicit state dependencies and a simulated user; open vs proprietary gap.
cite_claim: ToolSandbox evaluates stateful tool use with implicit dependencies between tools.
quote: ToolSandbox includes stateful tool execution, implicit state dependencies between tools
relevance: Related work; stateful substrate where read-after-write contracts are meaningful.

title: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) V4
authors: Gorilla team, UC Berkeley
central_claim: Function-calling accuracy leaderboard; V1 AST metric, V3 multi-turn, V4 holistic agentic evaluation; updated 2026-04-12.
cite_claim: BFCL evaluates whether models call functions accurately (AST-based), i.e. the call side, not the correctness of returned data.
location: Leaderboard page header and version history
quote: evaluates the LLM's ability to call functions (aka tools) accurately
relevance: Shows the dominant function-calling benchmark scores calls, not results; low fit for fiks.

title: Learning Evolving Tools for Large Language Models
authors: Guoxin Chen, Zhong Zhang, Xin Cong, Fangda Guo, Yesai Wu, Yankai Lin, Wenzheng Feng, Yasheng Wang
central_claim: Tools and APIs go stale as environments change; ToolEVO uses MCTS so the LLM self-reflects and adapts its tool usage; ToolQA-D benchmark of tool variability.
cite_claim: Prior work proposes making the agent adapt to evolving tools (ToolEVO, ToolQA-D), rather than fixing the tool.
quote: these tools and APIs may become outdated over time
relevance: Strongest competing framing (agent-side adaptation to drift). ToolQA-D is the closest existing 'API drift for agents' benchmark; its drift is visible (renamed APIs/params that error), unlike our silent drifts. Candidate baseline: agent-side adaptation without tool repair.

title: CodeUpdateArena: Benchmarking Knowledge Editing on API Updates
authors: Zeyu Leo Liu, Shrey Pandit, Xi Ye, Eunsol Choi, Greg Durrett
central_claim: 670 program-synthesis examples over synthetic updates to 54 functions in 7 Python packages; tests whether code LLMs absorb API updates.
cite_claim: Updating code LLMs' knowledge of API changes is harder than editing factual knowledge.
quote: Compared to knowledge editing for facts encoded in text, success here is more challenging
relevance: Library-evolution cluster: synthetic API updates are a precedent for seeded drift; measures model knowledge, not runtime detection.

title: GitChameleon: Unmasking the Version-Switching Capabilities of Code Generation Models
authors: Nizar Islah, Justine Gehring, Diganta Misra, Eilif Muller, Irina Rish, Terry Yue Zhuo, Massimo Caccia
central_claim: 116 version-specific Python completion problems with executable unit tests; GPT-4o and peers perform poorly.
cite_claim: Code LLMs struggle to generate code for a specific library version, measured by execution.
quote: The rapid evolution of software libraries presents a significant challenge for code generation models.
relevance: Library-evolution cluster; execution-based, but no runtime trace.

title: VersiCode: Towards Version-controllable Code Generation
authors: Tongtong Wu, Weigang Wu, Xingyu Wang, Kang Xu, Suyu Ma, Bo Jiang, Ping Yang, Zhenchang Xing, Yuan-Fang Li, Gholamreza Haffari
central_claim: Version-specific code completion and version-aware migration tasks; new CDC@1 metric; hard even for GPT-4o.
cite_claim: Version-aware code migration is a significant challenge even for frontier models.
quote: version-controllable code generation is indeed a significant challenge, even for GPT-4o and other strong frontier models.
relevance: Library-evolution cluster; migration task is the closest analogue to fiks's repair step but has no failing runtime trace.

title: CODESYNC: Synchronizing Large Language Models with Dynamic Code Evolution at Scale
authors: Chenlong Wang, Zhaoyang Chu, Zhengxiang Cheng, Xuyi Yang, Kaiyue Qiu, Yao Wan, Zhou Zhao, Xuanhua Shi, Dongping Chen
central_claim: Data engine for outdated API patterns; CODESYNCBENCH over 220 APIs in 6 libraries; 14 LLMs struggle even with DPO/ORPO/SimPO updates.
cite_claim: LLMs struggle with dynamic code evolution even after knowledge-updating methods.
quote: they struggle with dynamic code evolution
relevance: Supports the claim that the repair agent cannot rely on prior knowledge of upstream changes; the runtime trace supplies the new behavior.

title: BUMP: A Benchmark of Reproducible Breaking Dependency Updates
authors: Frank Reyes, Yogya Gamage, Gabriel Skoglund, Benoit Baudry, Martin Monperrus
central_claim: 571 executable breaking dependency updates from 153 Maven projects, containerized to reproduce the same build failure over time.
cite_claim: BUMP packages 571 breaking dependency updates so that each yields the same build failure reproducibly over time.
quote: BUMP ensures long-term reproducibility of dependency updates on different platforms, guaranteeing consistent build failures.
relevance: Closest repair benchmark in spirit (upstream change breaks client; repair client). Differences: compile-time, loud failures in Java; ours are runtime, silent, HTTP. Reproducibility-by-construction is the property our F gate also demands.

title: Byam: Fixing Breaking Dependency Updates with Large Language Models
authors: Frank Reyes, May Mahmoud, Federico Bono, Sarah Nadi, Benoit Baudry, Martin Monperrus
central_claim: LLM repair of client code broken by dependency updates on BUMP; o3-mini best, fully repairing 27% of builds and 78% of individual compilation errors.
cite_claim: On BUMP, the best LLM fully repaired 27% of broken builds while fixing 78% of individual compilation errors, i.e. partial repair is common.
quote: LLMs can automatically repair breaking updates.
relevance: External reference point for repair success on upstream-change breakage and for the partial-repair risk [C20]. [verify 27%/78% against the results table]

title: ToolFuzz -- Automated Agent Tool Testing
authors: Ivan Milev, Mislav Balunović, Maximilian Baader, Martin Vechev
central_claim: Generates diverse queries to find tool-documentation flaws that cause runtime errors or wrong agent answers; many public tools are underspecified.
cite_claim: Many publicly available agent tools suffer from underspecified documentation that leads to runtime errors or incorrect answers.
quote: We find that many publicly available tools suffer from underspecification.
relevance: Pre-deployment tool testing (fuzzing) is a competing approach; finds doc bugs offline, not behavioral drift in live traffic. Possible baseline for 'find the bug before traffic'.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
authors: Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, Karthik Narasimhan
central_claim: 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repos with fail-to-pass test evaluation; initial best model 1.96%.
cite_claim: Issue resolution is evaluated by fail-to-pass tests on real repositories (SWE-bench).
quote: a rich, sustainable, and challenging testbed for evaluating the next generation of language models
relevance: The F->P protocol our gates mirror; repair-side comparability anchor (C17, C18 build on it).

title: SWT-Bench: Testing and Validating Real-World Bug-Fixes with Code Agents
authors: Niels Mündler, Mark Niklas Müller, Jingxuan He, Martin Vechev
central_claim: Benchmark for turning user issues into reproducing tests; code-repair agents beat dedicated test generators; generated tests help filter fixes.
cite_claim: Generating issue-reproducing tests from issue text is a hard, measurable task (fail-to-pass rate), and such tests can filter candidate fixes.
quote: test generation remains relatively unexplored
relevance: Baseline protocol for H-repro: compare F->P validity of trace-derived tests vs tests generated from an issue description of the same bug.

title: TDD-Bench Verified: Can LLMs Generate Tests for Issues Before They Get Resolved?
authors: Toufique Ahmed, Martin Hirzel, Rangeet Pan, Avraham Shinnar, Saurabh Sinha
central_claim: 449 human-verified issues for test-first generation; Auto-TDD reaches a higher fail-to-pass rate than prior work.
cite_claim: Test-first reproduction from issue text is benchmarked by fail-to-pass rate on 449 verified issues.
quote: tests can clarify the desired behavior among stake-holders before anyone writes code for the agreed-upon fix
relevance: Second reference protocol for the reproduction step.

title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
authors: Sugam Panthi, Rabab Abdelfattah
central_claim: Contract checks + receipts naming recovery tools raise ToolMaze completion 10.9% -> 28.1% and τ-bench retail completion by 14.0 and 12.0 points under two injected get_order_details faults; detection outside mined vocabulary 46%.
cite_claim: On τ-bench retail with persistent injected get_order_details faults (status out of set; broken conservation), 50 of 115 tasks (seed 20260718), receipts raised completion by 14.0 and 12.0 points on two model tiers. [C11]
location: Abstract; Sec. 4 'τ-bench retail', 'ToolMaze Confirmation', 'Incident-derived faults'; Sec. 5; Appendices G and J; Limitations
quote: When a tool call times out, the agent sees the failure and can route around it.
relevance: Reuse C11. Closest prior evaluation: its τ-bench retail fault-injection protocol is the most comparable published setup for fiks's detection+receipt arm, and its baselines (schema-only, generic caution, always-verify) are directly reusable. Artifact license not stated.

title: From Confident Closing to Silent Failure: Characterizing False Success in LLM Agents
authors: Laksh Advani
central_claim: ~10,000 τ²-bench runs and ~1,900 AppWorld runs: false success is 45-48% of failures in single-control τ² domains, 3% in dual-control telecom; LLM judges AUROC <= 0.65; TF-IDF 0.83.
cite_claim: False success is 45-48% of failures in single-control τ²-bench domains but 3% in dual-control telecom; no LLM-judge configuration exceeded AUROC 0.65. [C7]
quote: LLM agents can fail silently by asserting task completion
relevance: Reuse C7. Establishes τ²-bench as the community substrate for silent-failure work and gives an LLM-judge baseline ceiling.

title: Reason Less, Verify More: Deterministic Gates Recover a Silent Policy-Violation Failure Mode in Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Vikas Reddy, Sumanth Reddy Challaram, Abhishek Basu
central_claim: On τ²-bench airline with gpt-4o-mini, 78% of failures were silent wrong-state errors; four deterministic pre-execution gates raised success 29.6% -> 42.0%, replicated on a disjoint seed set.
cite_claim: Deterministic read-only gates raised τ²-bench airline success from 29.6% to 42.0% (+12.4 pp), holding on a disjoint 15-seed set. [C8]
quote: Tool-using LLM agents can violate the very policies they are deployed to enforce
relevance: Reuse C8. Another τ² intervention with published effect sizes we can compare against.

title: Guardrails as Scapegoats: Auditing Unfaithful Safety Refusals in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
authors: Aarushi Singh
central_claim: Injects four silent failure profiles into 12 tool stubs; fabrication 56.6% of valid responses; safety language raises unfaithful refusals 15.6-fold.
cite_claim: With silent failure profiles injected into 12 tool stubs, agents fabricated results in 56.6% of valid responses. [C9]
quote: USR is a latent behavior, activated when safety vocabulary in the system prompt primes the model
relevance: Reuse C9. Its outcome coding (Honest Surrender / Fabrication / Unfaithful Safety Refusal) maps onto our grader (declined / wrong / correct) and could be adopted as a secondary metric.
